opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly my view on it has shifted a lot over the past year or so. The old intuition was that LoRA is the budget option. You use it when you can't afford full fine-tuning, and you accept that you're leaving performance on the table. For supervised fine-tuning on big datasets, that's often still true. If you're trying to cram a lot of new knowledge into a model, low-rank updates can bottleneck you.

RL is a different regime, though. The amount of information you're actually pushing into the model per episode is tiny. You roll out a bunch of attempts, you get back a scalar reward, maybe a few bits of signal per sample. You're not teaching the model a ton of new facts. You're mostly reshaping which behaviors it already has get upweighted. That kind of update is pretty naturally low-rank. So in practice, LoRA with a reasonable rank, and with the learning rate tuned for it, which matters a lot because LoRA usually wants a noticeably higher learning rate, tends to match full fine-tuning for RL much more closely than people expected.

Once you accept that, the infrastructure benefits get really compelling. With RL you're constantly moving weights between the trainer and the inference engine doing rollouts. Syncing a small adapter instead of the full model makes that loop way cheaper and faster. You can also serve many adapters off one base model, which is huge if you're running lots of experiments, or doing per-customer or per-task specialization. Multi-tenant RL starts to feel practical instead of crazy.

So my default these days is to start with LoRA for RL, especially for agentic or task-specific stuff where you're sharpening existing capabilities. I'd reach for full fine-tuning when you're doing something closer to mid-training: really long, large-scale runs where you expect the model to pick up genuinely new skills, or when you've run the experiment and actually see LoRA plateauing below where full fine-tuning gets. But I'd want that to come from an empirical comparison rather than an assumption, because a lot of the time the gap just isn't there.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that for most people doing RL today, LoRA is probably the right default, and the reasons are a little different from the reasons people usually give.

The common framing is "LoRA is cheaper but worse." And for supervised fine-tuning, where you're trying to cram a lot of new information or a lot of new behavior into the model, that's roughly true. You're fighting the model's priors, you want capacity, full fine-tuning wins. But RL is a different regime. The amount of actual signal you're getting per step in RL is tiny. You're getting a scalar reward, or a few bits of comparison, on a trajectory that might be thousands of tokens. So the information bandwidth of the training signal is really low, and a low-rank update is a pretty natural match for that. You're not really teaching the model new facts. You're nudging which of its existing behaviors it reaches for. The capacity argument just doesn't bite the same way.

And there's the stability side, which I think matters more in practice. RL is notoriously easy to blow up. Reward hacking, policy collapse, the model drifting off into weird degenerate outputs. Full fine-tuning gives the optimizer a lot of rope to hang itself with. LoRA is a built-in regularizer. You're constrained to a small subspace, which means it's harder to wander far from the base policy, and that's basically the same thing the KL penalty is trying to do for you anyway. So you often find that with LoRA you can get away with a looser KL term, or sometimes drop it, and the run just behaves better.

The practical stuff is also real. With RL you've got this awkward situation where you need a reference model, a policy, often a reward model, maybe a value model, all living in memory at once, plus you're doing generation, which is where most of the wall clock goes. LoRA means the reference and the policy share almost all their weights. Swapping adapters is cheap. You can serve rollouts off something like vLLM with the adapter hot-swapped in rather than re-syncing a full checkpoint every step. That changes what you can afford to do on a single node, and honestly a lot of the interesting experimentation happens at that scale.

Where I'd reach for full fine-tuning is when the RL is doing more than steering. If you're doing a very long run, lots of environments, trying to genuinely move the model's capabilities on something like math or code, then at some point you hit a ceiling with a low-rank update and you'll see the gap. The frontier labs are doing full fine-tuning for their big reasoning runs for a reason. But the gap tends to show up late and at scale, and most people are nowhere near that regime. They're trying to get a single environment to work on a single model and they're much more likely to die from instability than from lack of capacity.

So my rough heuristic is: start with LoRA, get the reward signal to actually go up, get the eval to actually go up, make sure you're not hacking the reward. Once that's all working and you're compute-constrained on the learning side rather than the debugging side, then try full fine-tuning and see if it buys you anything. A lot of the time it doesn't buy you as much as people expect.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it as a tradeoff between how quickly you can experiment and how much freedom you need to give the model to change. With LoRA, you’re training a relatively small set of parameters, so you save on optimizer memory and can often run experiments with less hardware. If the model already has the capabilities you need and you’re mostly trying to steer how it uses them, that’s a reasonable place to start.

Full fine-tuning gives you more flexibility, but it’s more expensive. And in reinforcement learning, the adapter isn’t necessarily the dominant cost—you may spend a lot of your compute generating rollouts. So I’d look at the whole training loop rather than assuming LoRA makes everything dramatically cheaper.

Practically, I’d start with LoRA, establish a baseline, and compare against full fine-tuning at a meaningful budget. If LoRA plateaus, I’d want to check whether that’s actually a capacity constraint or whether the reward, exploration, or training setup is the bottleneck. Giving the optimizer more parameters won’t automatically fix those problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of LoRA as a really useful starting point, especially if you’re trying to get an experiment running cheaply. You’re training a much smaller set of parameters, so the optimizer state is smaller, and that can make the whole setup easier to work with.

The question is whether that constraint gets in the way of what you want the model to learn. If you’re adapting behavior in a fairly narrow way, LoRA may be enough. If you’re trying to push the model substantially beyond its starting capabilities, I’d want to compare it against full fine-tuning rather than assume the adapter has enough capacity.

And for reinforcement learning, you have to look at the whole system. If most of your time is spent generating rollouts, making the training step cheaper doesn’t necessarily make the experiment dramatically cheaper. So I’d start with the simplest setup that lets me iterate, then compare learning curves and final performance at a realistic compute budget.
